programme.title: Arena
programme.sub-title: Dylan Thomas: From Grave to Cradle
programme.desc: Nigel Williams' 2003 profile of Swansea-born poet Dylan Thomas, whose work, especially his most famous piece Under Milk Wood, has influenced cultural icons such as John Lennon and Bob Dylan. The film tries to find out whether the basic elements of his legend are false - including the 18 whiskies that supposedly killed him in 1953 - and asks if the lurid stories prevent readers from truly understanding his poetry

programme.title: Life on Earth
programme.desc: David Attenborough has his famous encounter with a group of gorillas as he looks at the history of primates, whose ancestors sought their fortunes in the treetops. He reveals how they developed binocular vision for accurately judging distances, and the ability to grasp trees with a firm grip

programme.title: Great Railway Journeys
programme.desc: Michael Palin fulfils a boyhood dream to travel from London Euston to the Kyle of Lochalsh, near Skye, contrasting the world of modern trains with the nostalgic dreams of steam along the way. First broadcast in 1980

programme.title: Timeshift
programme.sub-title: Bridging the Gap: How the Severn Bridge Was Built
programme.desc: Liz Bonnin marks the 50th anniversary of the construction of the Severn Bridge in a Timeshift special telling the inside story of its design and construction. As the motorway link between England and Wales, the Severn Bridge was described as 'the most perfect suspension bridge in the world', and Liz reveals how its unique, slim-line structure came about by accident

programme.title: BBC Proms
programme.desc: Petroc Trelawny presents a concert from the Royal Albert Hall, which opens with Lahav Shani conducting the Munich Philharmonic in Louise Farrenc's dramatic Overture No 2. Pianist Argerich then joins the orchestra for Beethoven's Second Piano Concerto, before the programme concludes with Brahms' warm and joyful Brahms' Fourth Symphony

programme.title: Shelagh Delaney's Salford - Monitor
programme.desc: Ken Russell's portrait of Shelagh Delaney, originally broadcast in 1960, two months before her 21st birthday. The film provides an insight into the writer's native Salford, following her through bustling markets and past pubs, factories and terraced houses that were a key factor in the unique sense of community that informed her work. Introduced by Huw Wheldon

programme.title: Peter Egan Remembers - A Taste of Honey
programme.desc: The actor reflects on the 1984 adaptation of Shelagh Delaney's play, discussing the background to the drama and why it remains so powerful and still has such relevance today

programme.title: A Taste of Honey
programme.desc: A girl gets pregnant by a sailor and finds comfort with a gay friend. Michael Simpsons 1984 adaptation of Shelagh Delaney's play, starring Jane Freeman, Ian Targett, Peter Egan and Tony Armatrading

programme.title: Sian Phillips Remembers - Under Milk Wood
programme.desc: The actress looks back on Dylan Thomas's Under Milk Wood and her own experiences with various adaptations that have brought the poet's 'play for voices' to cinema and TV audiences. She recalls the BBC's 2014 version that brought together a huge range of Welsh talent including Tom Jones, Matthew Rhys, Charlotte Church, Michael Sheen and Katherine Jenkins. She also looks further back, sharing the story of her encounters with Dylan Thomas, and her part in the 1972 film, which saw her working alongside her then-husband Peter O'Toole, Richard Burton, his wife Elizabeth Taylor

programme.title: Under Milk Wood
programme.desc: Star-studded performance of Dylan Thomas's radio play from locations across New York, Los Angeles, London, Cardiff and Laugharne. Michael Sheen opens as First Voice, with Tom Jones as Captain Cat, and as each of Dylan's characters joins in, the piece builds into a collage of famous voices and faces. They include Matthew Rhys, Ioan Gruffudd, Sian Phillips, Jonathan Pryce, Bryn Terfel, Katherine Jenkins, Griff Rhys Jones, Charlotte Church, Robert Pugh, Eve Myles, Owen Teale and Kimberley Nixon. The words are intercut with evocative imagery inspired by the play, while the performance was created as part of a live event by National Theatre Wales

programme.title: Nature and Us: A History Through Art
programme.desc: James Fox uses art to explore how humans began to try to understand nature for the very first time. From the Song dynasty in China and the Islamic world, through to the Scientific Revolution and the advent of the industrial era, he shows the very different ways in which humans came to both appreciate and understand nature

programme.title: Shelagh Delaney's Salford - Monitor
programme.desc: Ken Russell's portrait of Shelagh Delaney, originally broadcast in 1960, two months before her 21st birthday. programme.title: The Architecture the Railways Built
programme.desc: Tim Dunn takes a look at the architecture of the Stockton and Darlington railway, the first passenger steam line in the world and learns how Essex's enormous Chappel Viaduct was built

programme.title: The Flying Gardener
programme.desc: Chris Beardshaw takes to the air in his helicopter and heads for Cornwall to create a tropical paradise in a school's backyard, regardless of weather and soil conditions. Along the way he takes a dip in the ocean in search of plants washed in from South America, and visits Britain's very own Jurassic Park

programme.title: Archaeology: A Secret History
programme.desc: Richard Miles concludes his series charting the history of archaeological breakthroughs by discovering more about the ancient common man. The investigation takes the archaeologist from the elaborate grave of Egyptian boy king Tutankhamun to the Danish resting place of the Tollund Man, who died as part of an Iron Age sacrifice more than 2,000 years ago

programme.title: Classic Mastermind
programme.desc: Magnus Magnusson hosts the fifth heat of the quiz, with specialist subjects of the Spanish anarchist movement 1908-1975, the operas of Benjamin Britten, the history of the Royal Navy 1794-1805, and the Berry novels of Dornford Yates

programme.title: Call My Bluff
programme.desc: Robert Robinson presides over another duel of words and wits as Jenny Agutter, Sinead Cusack, Tim Rice and Nigel Dempster join team captains Frank Muir and Patrick Campbell. First broadcast in 1978

programme.title: The Search for the Lost Manuscript: Julian of Norwich
programme.desc: Historian Janina Ramirez tells the story of the first book written in English by a woman, Revelations of Divine Love by Julian of Norwich. The book was written in 1373 and presents an alternative viewpoint on man's relationship with God, which led to it being suppressed for more than 500 years. She travels from Norwich to Cambrai in Northern France, revealing how the book survived and the stories of women who championed it, and consults with academics and theologians about the book's importance

programme.title: Romancing the Stone: The Golden Ages of British Sculpture
programme.desc: Alastair Sooke examines the three 'golden ages' of British sculpture and the technical breakthroughs that made them possible. He begins with a look at the Norman ecclesiastical building programme and the masterworks created by anonymous medieval masons and artisans to the glory of God - until Henry VIII's Reformation brought wholesale destruction

programme.title: The Secret Rules of Modern Living: Algorithms
programme.desc: Without people noticing, modern life has been taken over. Algorithms run everything, from search engines on the internet, to satnavs and credit-card security - they even help people travel the world, find love and save lives. Here, mathematician Marcus du Sautoy demystifies this hidden world by showing some of the most essential algorithms. He reveals where these 2,000-year-old problem-solvers came from, showing how they work, what they have achieved and how they are now so advanced they can even program themselves

programme.desc: As the Titanic started to sink in April 1912, another ship came into view, offering her passengers the hope of being rescued. However, despite a fusillade of rockets, the ship turned away. Within two hours, 1,500 people were dead. An American investigation at the time accused the SS Californian, even though the freighter was stationary that night. A British inquiry concurred, keen to shift blame from national failures on lifeboat provision and steamship supervision. However, since Titanic's wreck was discovered, the mystery began to unlock, and now, with recently discovered clues, a new suspect has emerged: the SS Mount Temple. In the first of two programmes, she explores the conditions of their tightly packed houses, how they dressed and what they ate. Joann also examines their love of poetry, their enthusiasm for interior design and what it was like to work in the Valley of the Kings, where the pharaohs were entombed

programme.title: Ancient Egypt: Life and Death in the Valley of the Kings
programme.desc: Part two of two. Joann Fletcher investigates the Ancient Egyptian attitude to death, revealing that to them life was just a dress rehearsal for the perfect afterlife that they were trying to reach. Joann clambers into rarely visited tombs, explores a treasure trove of long-buried objects and examines mummies to discover just why they spent a fortune preparing for death - and what they hoped to find when they got there

programme.title: Cleopatra
programme.desc: Part one of two. Dramatised documentary recounting the life of the iconic Egyptian ruler. By the age of 21, Cleopatra had already seen her sister killed by their own father. She became queen of Egypt before escaping almost certain death. Outcast from the royal family and knowing she had nothing to lose, so set about seducing Julius Caesar to ensure the survival of both her dynasty and Egypt itself

programme.title: The Middle

American comedy, starring Patricia Heaton, Neil Flynn, Atticus Shaffer and Charlie McDermott

programme.title: The Middle

programme.title: The Middle

programme.title: The Green Planet
programme.desc: David Attenborough presents a guide to the lives of plants in environments around the world, beginning with the plant battlegrounds of the tropical rainforests. New filming techniques allow viewers to enter the plants' world and see it from their perspective, and on their timescale. Featuring fast-growing trees, flowers that mimic dead animals, and life and death battles to absorb much-needed sunlight

programme.title: The Green Planet
programme.desc: David Attenborough presents a guide to the world of plants that grow in water, including a bubbling river in Brazil, where the plants have created their own atmosphere and a lake smothered in brightly-coloured flowers. Plus, plants that fight each other for growing space or use natural adhesives to prevent themselves being swept downstream, and a look at the methods used to evade or even attack animals

programme.title: The Green Planet
programme.desc: The strategy, deception and feats of engineering plants use to thrive in the changing weather of different seasons. In the face of conditions ranging from ice and snow to raging fires, survival is often a question of perfect timing - particularly when contending with intense competition and surprising predators

programme.title: The Green Planet
programme.desc: Plants that have developed to thrive in the desert, including cacti that grow in the shade of other trees and collect water in pleated trunks that expand and contract - but can also find themselves a host to other plants, like desert mistletoe. The programme also reveals how tobacco plants being eaten by caterpillars are able to summon the creatures' natural predators, and how tumbleweeds roll across the landscape, only unfurling and growing when they encounter rain

programme.title: Killer Women with Piers Morgan

Later, Piers travels to meet Seath's parents in Summerfield, Florida, with their visceral anger standing in stark contrast to Amber's cool demeanour. It soon emerges that Amber was a central player in the plot to kill Seath, but will she take responsibility for her actions?

programme.desc: Armed with his trusty 1913 Bradshaw's Continental Railway Guide, Michael Portillo travels east through the Balkans along the most exotic section of the route taken by the Orient Express. His journey begins in Sofia, capital of Bulgaria, and includes stops in the ancient city of Plovdiv, the region of Rumelia, and former capital of the Ottoman Empire Edirne. Arriving in Istanbul, Michael takes a trip on the Bosphorus - a much-coveted stretch of water - finds out about Turkish delight and travels along the Marmaray metro line, which connects European and Asian Istanbul via a tunnel beneath the Bosphorus

programme.title: Great Continental Railway Journeys
programme.desc: In Vienna, Michael Portillo encounters a pre-Cold War spy and learns about the concert that caused a riot in 1913. He then travels the Habsburg imperial line across the Semmering Pass, a line blasted through the Alps. In Graz, the former politician ventures underground at the Lurgrotte Caves to find out about a famous rescue operation of the past, then in Slovenia discovers how an earthquake in Ljubljana prompted its citizens to assert their national identity in architecture and art. Arriving in the Italian port of Trieste, Michael savours the imported coffee that fuelled a cafe culture

programme.desc: Armed with his trusty 1913 Bradshaw's Continental Railway Guide, Michael Portillo travels east through the Balkans along the most exotic section of the route taken by the Orient Express. His journey begins in Sofia, capital of Bulgaria, and includes stops in the ancient city of Plovdiv, the region of Rumelia, and former capital of the Ottoman Empire Edirne. Arriving in Istanbul, Michael takes a trip on the Bosphorus - a much-coveted stretch of water - finds out about Turkish delight and travels along the Marmaray metro line, which connects European and Asian Istanbul via a tunnel beneath the Bosphorus

programme.title: Great Continental Railway Journeys
programme.desc: In Vienna, Michael Portillo encounters a pre-Cold War spy and learns about the concert that caused a riot in 1913. He then travels the Habsburg imperial line across the Semmering Pass, a line blasted through the Alps. In Graz, the former politician ventures underground at the Lurgrotte Caves to find out about a famous rescue operation of the past, then in Slovenia discovers how an earthquake in Ljubljana prompted its citizens to assert their national identity in architecture and art. Arriving in the Italian port of Trieste, Michael savours the imported coffee that fuelled a cafe culture
